summary.text: Melting, also called fusion, is the phase transition in which a substance changes from a solid to a liquid.
It happens when the solid's internal energy rises, usually from heat or pressure, until the ordered arrangement of its ions or molecules breaks down at the melting point.
Melting is a first-order transition: free energy does not change at the melting point, but enthalpy and entropy do, which is where latent heat comes from.

facts.label: Supercooling record
facts.value: Fine water droplets cooled to -38 °C without freezing

facts.label: Odd viscosity
facts.value: Molten sulfur gets thicker between 130 and 190 °C

facts.label: Pre-melting
facts.value: Thin liquid-like films form on crystal surfaces below the melting point

items.prompt: A crystal is warmed until it reaches its melting point. What happens to its internal arrangement there?

options.label: The atoms stop vibrating and lock in place
The ordered pattern breaks down to a looser state
The atoms pack into an even tighter pattern
The atoms split apart into separate particles

items.explain: At the melting point the ordering of ions or molecules breaks down to a less ordered state.

items.prompt: Water sits on a very clean glass surface several degrees below freezing and has not frozen. Why can it stay that way?

options.label: No disturbance sets off the change in the still water
Glass permanently lowers the temperature water freezes at
Glass quietly warms the water back to its freezing point
Cold water is simply more stable as a liquid

items.explain: Freezing needs a trigger from fluctuations or disturbances; if the material is kept still, supercooling can persist.

items.prompt: Two labs melt the same solid, one at sea level and one at much higher pressure. What should they expect?

options.label: The same temperature, since melting depends only on the material
The same temperature, since only boiling responds to pressure
Possibly different melting temperatures, set partly by pressure
Different results only if heating speeds differ

items.explain: The temperature at which melting occurs depends on the ambient pressure.

items.prompt: By the Lindemann idea, what pushes a crystal over the edge into melting as it heats up?

options.label: Its atoms run out of room to vibrate at all
Its bonds suddenly become much stronger
Its atoms start to bunch closer together
Its atoms' vibrations grow large next to their spacing

items.explain: The Lindemann criterion says melting is a vibrational instability when thermal vibration amplitude is large relative to the distances between atoms.

items.prompt: Why is melting counted as a first-order transition?

options.label: Free energy stays put, yet enthalpy and entropy change
It is the first change any solid goes through
Enthalpy stays put, yet free energy changes sharply
It only occurs at exactly one atmosphere

items.explain: At the melting point the free energy change is zero but enthalpy and entropy change, giving latent heat, which makes it first-order.

items.prompt: Helium-3 below 0.3 K is a rare exception to how melting usually works. What is needed to melt it at a suitable constant pressure?

options.label: A great deal more energy than usual
Its pressure dropped to nearly zero
It must first be turned into a gas
Energy must be withdrawn from it

items.explain: Helium-3 has a negative enthalpy of fusion at those temperatures, so heat must be removed to melt it.
